articles.title: Recovery Key storage transition highlights Apple’s privacy and obscurity
articles.subtitle: We trust Apple with a lot of our data. In general, that hasn’t seemed like a bad idea; in particular, compared to its competitors, Apple seems to ensure that it can inspect or interact with very little of our data.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
We trust Apple with a lot of our data. In general, that hasn’t seemed like a bad idea; in particular, compared to its competitors, Apple seems to ensure that it can inspect or interact with very little of our data. The company has built its platform and its reputation on being an elegant, frictionless, hands-off conduit.

While we can make many complaints about Liquid Glass, its increased focus on invasive (and poor) advertising, its software quality, and much else, Apple has kept its corporate nose cleaner than anybody else. Its transparency and documentation are, oddly, worse than its actions and clear intent.

I was thinking about this when I received an email from an anonymized iCloud Hide My Email account, asking for more detail about how Apple managed the transition from the old method of presenting or escrowing (in iCloud) your macOS FileVault Recovery Key to the new method, in which the key is stored in Passwords. This transition, which I’ve documented in a few places, was a step forward in privacy and security.

But not transparency! I’ll explain, but you can’t find an explanation on Apple’s site about the transition. The support documentation remains out of sync with Tahoe. That leaves it to yours truly to explicate.

Don’t trust and verify

The Electronic Frontier Foundation recently published a newsletter with a round-up of how fitness wearables, like rings, watches, and bands, preserve your privacy from government intrusion, as well as whether they protect you from unwanted security invasions by using end-to-end encryption (E2EE). (The former often requires the latter: governments typically can’t break through E2EE.)

I want to quote two full paragraphs to make this point:

In the end, we found that only four of these companies (Apple, Google, Whoop, and Oura) promise to notify users of law enforcement requests in publicly available documentation. And just two of those companies, Apple and Google (which also owns Fitbit), currently publish transparency reports on how often they hand users’ data to the government.

Support for end-to-end encryption—a method that ensures your personal data is only accessible by you, and not the company who makes the device and manages the cloud storage—is more rare than transparency reports among wearable device makers. The Apple Watch is the only popular fitness wearable that supports end-to-end encryption. 1

In the end, we found that only four of these companies (Apple, Google, Whoop, and Oura) promise to notify users of law enforcement requests in publicly available documentation. And just two of those companies, Apple and Google (which also owns Fitbit), currently publish transparency reports on how often they hand users’ data to the government.

Support for end-to-end encryption—a method that ensures your personal data is only accessible by you, and not the company who makes the device and manages the cloud storage—is more rare than transparency reports among wearable device makers. The Apple Watch is the only popular fitness wearable that supports end-to-end encryption. 1

Apple wasn’t an early player with E2EE. Really, it was seen as the kind of thing only true security geeks cared about, even while people like EFF and other digital privacy advocacy groups and individuals warned us that our data was only lightly protected. Over time, as the criminal, exploitative, and political monitoring and extraction of our secrets became clear, Apple kept stepping up.

The Secure Enclave is a keystone of those moves, as the tamper-resistant silicon subsystem allows devices to keep locally generated security keys entirely private. Most of these keys never leave the Secure Enclave! Rather, it’s the encryption hub. 2

iCloud initially had a fairly cursory level of protection, with the then-Apple ID account password serving as the only real bar. Two-step verification in March 2013 provided better account protection, but didn’t cover iCloud backups, which could be retrieved without that second step. A rash of celebrity account leaks in late summer 2014 led Apple to extend two-step to iCloud data within a couple of weeks.

The next year, it upgraded security to the more rigorous two-factor authentication, which later became mandatory.

As part of its response to the iCloud data hijacks, Apple began to beef up iCloud. It began rolling out E2EE for all the device-based services it could, leaving synced data still relatively lightly protected. (iCloud data is always encrypted with Apple’s at-rest keys, which only it ostensibly has access to, and in transit with HTTPS. However, a security breach at Apple or someone able to hijack one end of an in-progress HTTPS sync allows access to that unencrypted data.)

Then, suddenly, months after shipping major updates to its operating systems, Apple announced Advanced Data Protection in December 2022. Enabling this feature put the E2EE aegis over nearly all synced or stored data at iCloud; mail, contacts, and calendar entries remain an exception because of their interoperability with third-party apps and services. You can view Apple’s document that explains what level of protection applies to data, with and without ADP enabled.

With that in mind, let’s talk about the Recovery Key transition.

Claude Code has a new simulator button.

Claude Code’s Mac desktop app has added Apple simulator support, and although it’s billed as “iOS Simulator Support,” it actually works with any iOS, iPadOS, visionOS, or watchOS simulator you have installed.

The process of setting up a simulator is simple. A new button with an iPhone icon appears when you open an existing project. Click it and a new iPhone simulator pane opens to the right by default. However, clicking on the name of the simulator reveals a list of every available simulator. You can also run multiple simulators at once, but that immediately made my aging M1 Max Mac Studio start to chug a little.

With access to your running app, Claude Code is more effective at debugging UI bugs.

Once you have the simulators that you want open, simply ask Claude Code to run and test your app, and it gets to work, building the app, installing it in the simulator, opening it, and poking around. I loaded up a simple word game I’ve been playing with, and after a few minutes, Claude Code found a UI bug while controlling the simulator. I asked it to fix the issue, which it did, then tested and committed. My testing has been limited, but so far it looks like a simple, effective loop.

It’s also worth noting that Claude Code is running the simulator directly inside the Claude app. This is not computer use, meaning windows aren’t going to be opening and getting in your way as you work on something else. All in all, the addition of the simulator, like the inclusion of an in-app sandboxed browser a couple of weeks ago, is a great update to Claude Code.

articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Saber Interactive CEO said he would have 'been happy' to replace a former employee with AI

Related

Saber Interactive CEO Matthew Karch is making his stance on AI very clear. In a statement to IGN, he said that the publisher won’t be “shying away” from AI-powered features like generative speech and text in the company’s upcoming game Rideshare Stimulator. He added that he would have “been happy” to have replaced a former writer who worked for Saber with AI.

Controversy around the upcoming Rideshare Stimulator began earlier this week when the game’s former lead writer, Stella Sacco, wrote that she was replaced by ChatGPT partway through development. She posted on Bluesky in response to the game’s reveal, “I didn’t even see this had been announced. I was lead writer on this one! And Saber replaced me with ChatGPT midway through development.

All the passenger voices were AI too. Either they changed direction at some point or they’re not disclosing it on Steam. ” Rideshare Stimulator still doesn’t currently have Steam's required AI disclosure on the platform.

Saber Interactive denied the claim in a statement to PC Gamer, saying, “Neither Saber nor Unigine have replaced any writers with AI for Rideshare or any other game.” However, they went on to clarify that Sacco was correct that the game does use generative AI, and it will feature a previously undisclosed “free ride” mode that has “infinite” passengers.

Sacco pushed back on the claim she wasn't replaced by the technology, saying to PC Gamer, “I was there, and it was my job to write the game, and then it wasn’t once Matt Karch decided using ChatGPT would be great publicity for the game.”

My boss, to his credit, argued over and over with the c-level who pushed the AI — “we already have Stella and she’s funny and she’s good at this, she’s done live games before so live ops are no problem,” etc — but the suit insisted “gamers love new tech” so using AI would be “great marketing” — Stella Sacco (@antlervel.vet) 2026-08-11T16:40:32.103Z

In response, Karch took a combative tone in a statement to This Week In Video Games, “Stella who? I had to ask Claude because I have never spoken to her or seen her. We have already said we are using AI for certain parts of the game and will update the Steam page once we have finalized the feature set.”

“As far as Stella is concerned, she was replaced by someone more talented and terminated for a variety of reasons a few months later. From what I can gather she enjoys controversy even more than I do. I would frankly in retrospect have been happy to replace her with AI. At least we would be dealing with someone programmed to be honest.”

"I’ve seen the statement by Matt Karch, the CEO of Saber Entertainment, and all of the truly horrendous things he said about me," Sacco responded in This Week In Video Games. "I think it should be obvious to anyone who reads that statement that he’s lashing out because he did not want people to know there was AI use in the game.”

She added, “Everything I said was true. Here’s more truth: that statement is remarkably pathetic for the CEO of any company to be making, and combined with the AI use it will do far more damage to Saber’s reputation than it ever could mine. This screed will be many people’s first exposure to the Saber brand.”

This isn’t the first time Karch has made controversial statements. He recently admitted to taking a “dig” at Gearbox CEO Randy Pitchford in the announcement trailer for Rideshare Stimulator, and said that “Without Embracer, Randy is performing magic tricks at birthday parties for a living.”

After the release of Saber Interactive's Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine 2, YouTuber Asmongold made a video praising the game — for those unfamiliar with Asmongold, he is a right-wing content creator who was banned from Twitch after saying that Palestinians are part of an “inferior culture” in response to the Israeli military bombing civilians in Gaza.

Karch appeared to post a comment on Asmongold’s Space Marine 2 video saying, “Hey man, CEO of Saber here. I love your videos. ” He added, “I hope that games like Space Marine 2 and Wukong are the start of a reversion to a time when games were simply about fun and immersion.

I spent some time as Chief Operating Officer at Embracer and I saw games there that made me want to cry with their overblown attempts at messaging or imposing morals on gamers. ” Many perceived the phrase “imposing morals on gamers” as an “anti-woke” dogwhistle, the kind used by right-wing culture warriors whenever minorities or women are playable characters in video games.

In the video, Asmongold railed against the game Dustborn, which was a common target of right-wing reactionaries at the time for its diverse cast.

Saber refused to clarify whether Karch’s comment on the Asmongold video belonged to the CEO, but Karch later wrote on LinkedIn that “whoever wrote that seems pretty sharp.”

articles.subtitle: Your voice may be your passport, as a certain Robert Redford picture once asserted, but two macOS apps in our spotlight this week view your voice as a way to get more things done on your Mac.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
Your voice may be your passport, as a certain Robert Redford picture once asserted, but two macOS apps in our spotlight this week view your voice as a way to get more things done on your Mac. We’re talking transcription apps with two apps that take very different approaches to what you can do with vocal recognition and AI.

But that’s not all for this week. We also look at a tool to help you better enjoy email newsletters, an iPhone app for making your photos sound as good as ever and a multiplatform game that helps you fine-tune your puzzle-solving skills.

Got an app of your own that you’d like to see highlighted? Let us know at apps@sixcolors.com with a brief description of what it does, and we’ll take it from there.

Vox Dictum

I record a lot of interviews, which means I need to transcribe a lot of interviews, and so far, I’ve found the Apple Intelligence tools built into Apple’s various software platforms to be fairly wanting in this area. So when an app like Vox Dictum promises a better transcription experience, I’m all ears.

Vox Dictum is a macOS app that makes privacy its calling card — all the transcription happens directly on your Mac, as do the AI-powered summary features that you can access with the cost of a subscription. A Pro subscription costs $7.99/month and gets you features like large AI models to download to your Mac plus AI summaries while the $12.99/month Pro+ package adds a speaker recognition feature.

I do think it’s easier to label speakers in VoxDictum than with any of Apple’s built-in features, though transcripts — while fairly accurate — feature line breaks that aren’t necessarily suited to my purposes.

As for the summary feature, I found it to be hit-and-miss: Vox Dictum did a great job highlighting the main points of an interview I conducted for a freelance article, making the summary a good reference tool, but a recorded discussion between me and my wife produced a summary with conflicting dates on some action items. That said, I do like that Vox Dictum’s summary feature lets you designate if the recording is an interview, a meeting, a news bulletin or a podcast, which seems to help focus the summary.

Processing time can take a bit, but if you find yourself needing to transcribe a lot of interviews, Vox Dictum is definitely worth a download so you can see if its base features improve on your current approach.

Bonfiyah

Like Vox Dictum, Bonfiyah promises to turn recordings into transcripts, while also recognizing who’s saying what. But transcription is really just a sideshow in this case — the app’s real strength lies in its ability to track your conversations.

Available for the iPhone, iPad and Mac — I tried out the macOS version — Bonfiyah records conversations, meetings and brainstorming sessions. (You can also import audio files into the app. ) Besides transcription and speaker identification features, the app also taps into AI to summarize action items that come up in your conversation and who’s responsible for taking care of them.

A feature I particularly like is an analysis tool that analyzes how to communicate more effectively with the people you talk to on a regular basis.

Transcription does take place off-device via AssemblyAI, though Bonfiyah deletes that info from its servers after seven days. The app includes privacy features such as marking conversations as privileged.

Bonfiyah comes across as a pretty sophisticated tool that might be overkill for anyone who needs transcripts with more basic summary features. But you can try out all the features to start with for 14 days before you need to commit to either a $24.99/month Pro or $34.99/month Pro AI account for more advanced features.

Letterboxx

Letterboxx exists under the premise that an email inbox is no place to enjoy a newsletter and a traditional mail client is not a reader app. Inboxes are places for taking action like responding to timely messages, but newsletters are something that you want to spend time diving into — hence the Letterboxx interface, which is designed to use the ample space provided on your Mac.

With Letterboxx, you can redirect newsletters sent to supported email accounts to a dedicated reading space, complete with folders for organizing incoming missives by type. You also get ad-filtering tools, ways to highlight relevant text and even shortcuts for managing your many subscriptions.

articles.title: macOS 27 Golden Gate: The MacStories Public Beta Preview
articles.subtitle: The public beta of macOS 27 Golden Gate is out today, and I’m sure many of you are wondering whether to take the plunge and give it a try in advance of its official fall release. That’s the question this preview is here to help answer.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
The public beta of macOS 27 Golden Gate is out today, and I’m sure many of you are wondering whether to take the plunge and give it a try in advance of its official fall release. That’s the question this preview is here to help answer.

It’s not my final take on Golden Gate by any means; after all, I’ve only been using it for about a month, and there will be several more turns in the beta cycle between now and the public release. However, I’ve used Golden Gate long enough to help you make an informed decision about whether or not to install the public beta now.

Of course, it’s impossible for me to account for everyone’s unique Mac setups when considering Golden Gate’s stability, but it’s worth reiterating what I’ve said in past previews: modern Apple betas have been consistently stable. That’s to say, the risks of using the public beta are modest. It’s been years since I’ve had a critical app fail or lost data.

I never go into beta season without a backup plan, though. If something goes terribly wrong, I have backups, backups of those backups, and alternate Macs I can switch to in the event of a disaster. I don’t expect to have to go to Plan B, but if you’re going to jump on the Beta Bus, you should have a Plan B, too.

Okay, you’ve been warned. Let’s get to the fun part.

Supported By

Inoreader

Every year’s macOS update is a little different, but Golden Gate is more different than most. Instead of focusing on tentpole features and apps (with the exception of a new Siri app), macOS 27’s updates fall into three broad categories:

refinements to Apple’s Liquid Glass design language,

hundreds of system-level changes intended to improve your Mac’s performance, and

Apple Intelligence, which includes the new Siri app as well as many other AI additions to existing system apps.

It’s been a while since the “Snow Leopard Moment.”

With so many past macOS updates focusing on system apps, it’s refreshing to see Apple take a more holistic system-level approach, which harkens back to how most people remember OS X Snow Leopard. In fact, during WWDC briefings, Apple representatives likened the Golden Gate update to Snow Leopard before anyone in the room even asked about it.

Snow Leopard is remembered as a release that focused on performance over features. The reality is that the update also introduced its fair share of new features, but many were less splashy from a user-facing standpoint. They were under-the-hood updates that made the Mac work better without users having to think about it much. In that sense, Golden Gate has a lot in common with Snow Leopard.

Other than the brand new Siri app, you probably won’t notice that much is different when you first launch the new version. But over time, the changes will reveal themselves, adding up to a whole that – with few exceptions – is greater than the parts.

So let’s take a closer look at how Liquid Glass has evolved, the most significant system changes, and what it’s like to use Siri and other Apple Intelligence updates in Golden Gate’s public beta.

Design

Windows stand out from each other more, and the sidebar runs edge to edge in Golden Gate.

articles.title: Apple’s AI announcements: One big question, and 11 key features
articles.subtitle: Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form. The company had a lot of ground to make up.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form.

The company had a lot of ground to make up. Obviously, the test will be how well the new features work in real life usage, but let’s start with what seemed to me to be the most important things the company announced …

The big iPhone support question

For me, one of the biggest questions to arise from the keynote was exactly what features will require the iPhone 17 Pro and up?

Apple had three things to say about iPhone support. The first says that any phone capable of running iOS 26 can be upgraded to iOS 27. That means all the way back to the iPhone 11.

The second is that the new AI features only extend back to the iPhone 15 Pro:

Apple Intelligence and Siri AI in iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27, and visionOS 27 are available on iPhone 16 models or later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max.

The third says that some features are limited to just the latest and greatest models.

Apple’s most powerful on-device model and the features it enables, like expressive voices and more advanced dictation, are available on iPhone Air, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max.

The word ‘like’ is doing a lot of heavy lifting there: it means we don’t yet know what other features will fall into this category. Additionally, it’s not yet 100% clear whether phones that can’t perform these actions on-device will still get access to the same features, just relying on cloud connectivity.

This latter question is especially important when it comes to advanced dictation. However smart the new Siri may be, it first needs to understand what we are saying. The existing Siri speech-to-text capabilities fall way short of what is available from third-parties.

The overall model seems well-considered

Apple’s general approach here is to make Siri’s new capabilities transparently available system-wide. In other words, we can ask our iPhone to do something and the new Siri will step in to perform the task.

However, there are times when it’s useful to revisit an earlier chatbot session, and Apple allows us to do this through the Siri app. That seems to me the best of both worlds. We don’t need to open Siri to do anything requiring the new Apple Intelligence features, but we can access past sessions when required.

Agentic AI is key

The ability to ask our iPhone to carry out a task and have it be able to access not only the personal information we have stored on our phone, but also interact with apps, is absolutely key to truly useful AI.

Again, we will need to see how well this really works, but Apple does seem to be ticking all of the boxes in terms of the capabilities I was looking for.

Privacy is core

articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
It's time to transfer any Pokémon to the newer Home service if you don't want to lose them

Related

If you moved Pokémon into Pokémon Bank years ago to store them for a rainy day, now is the time to retrieve them. The Pokémon Company has announced that it will be ending the service on Nintendo 3DS in 2027, over a decade after it first launched.

The Pokémon Company announced the closure of the Bank service on Thursday in a new blog post about the Pokémon Home service, Bank's successor. Support for Pokémon Bank will officially end on Thursday, Feb. 25, 2027 at 7 p.m. PST.

Launched in Japan in 2013 and globally in 2014, Pokémon Bank is a 3DS app that serves as a storage and transfer hub players can use with any Pokémon game on the handheld. While the service initially required a subscription, it has been free to use for those who had already downloaded it by the time Nintendo shut down the 3DS eShop in 2023.

The Pokémon Company advises those who still have Pokémon stored in Bank to transfer them to the modern Home service as soon as possible. Once you transfer Pokémon from Bank to Home, the Pokémon cannot be moved back to Bank. Transferring Pokémon between Bank and Home can be a long, complicated process, so check out our detailed guide for help. To make the move easier, an October update to Home will increase the number of Pokémon that Premium Plan subscribers can deposit to 9,000.

Unfortunately, the process can require multiple systems, games, and apps that are no longer available in some cases. Still, if you have everything you need, now is the time to save your beloved pocket monsters. If normal channels don't work, dedicated fans have alternative solutions available if you know where to look.

Fan sentiment around the announcement has been fairly somber. While many understand this was a long time coming, it doesn't lessen the frustration of yet another service for preserving digital memories being shuttered. Pokémon ignited many gamers' love for the medium, and the attachment they form to beloved creatures is something that should be easier to preserve.

articles.title: Review: “Ted Lasso” returns, refreshed, to the pitch
articles.subtitle: Tanya Reynolds and Jason Sudeikis in “Ted Lasso.” “Ted Lasso” is back on Apple TV, which was no sure thing after the series more or less wrapped up in May of 2023.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
“Ted Lasso” is back on Apple TV, which was no sure thing after the series more or less wrapped up in May of 2023. But it’s back for a fourth season, in which—after an episode-long visit to Ted’s home of Kansas City—the football-turned-soccer coach returns to Richmond, where—as teased at the end of season 3—a new women’s team is launching and just might need a coach.

I’ve seen the first half of the season, and I’m happy to report that though the teams have changed, this is still “Ted Lasso” through and through. Thematically the first three seasons were about Ted’s journey in running away from a dissolving marriage. With season four, a whole new set of themes begin to emerge.

Yes, love ’em or hate ’em Ted’s homespun aphorisms still abound. The relationship between owner Rebecca and marketing genius Keely continues to be as strong as ever. Higgins is still doing his Higgins stuff. Mae is still tending bar. Those three fans in the pub are as random as ever.

But in coaching a barely-formed women’s team that is in desperate need of players and fans, “Ted Lasso” returns to its roots as an underdog story, which helps make the whole thing feel more like the show’s first season. (There’s even a press conference scene that is disastrous for entirely different reasons from the original. )

It’s great to have series co-creator Brendan Hunt back as Coach Beard, but the addition of Tanya Reynolds (“Sex Education”) as Alice Chilton introduces a new dynamic. Chilton is the only coach who can go into the locker room without permission, she thinks she deserves the managerial job, and she’s got some serious anger control problems. Reynolds adds a lot of grit to the proceedings, preventing it from becoming too much of a sickeningly sweet reunion love-fest.

The character least served from the season, at least so far as I’ve seen, is breakout character Roy Kent (Brett Goldstein). He’s there and has some moments, but since he’s the manager of the men’s team, he’s often relegated being a gruff, bearded question mark attached to questions about his relationship status with Keeley.

I appreciate the ironic turnabout of the men’s manager being an afterthought who’s only relevant in terms of his romantic storylines, but I do wonder if Roy is too strong of a character to be served in such limited doses.

Anyway, the best review I can give to season four of “Ted Lasso” is that each episode made me laugh out loud, a lot. Not only was it nice to see these familiar characters again, but the show did the most important job any comedy has—it’s funny. Welcome back, coach.

articles.subtitle: You're gonna have to work for the Mythical Pokémon, though Related As part of Pokémon 's 30th anniversary celebrations in 2026, the classic Gen 1 remakes Pokémon FireRed and Pokémon LeafGreen were ported to the Nintendo Switch and Nintendo Switch 2 for...
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
You're gonna have to work for the Mythical Pokémon, though

Related

As part of Pokémon 's 30th anniversary celebrations in 2026, the classic Gen 1 remakes Pokémon FireRed and Pokémon LeafGreen were ported to the Nintendo Switch and Nintendo Switch 2 for $19.99 each. However, like so many other Pokémon releases, they didn't launch with the ability to move creatures to Pokémon Home. That changes this October when Pokémon FireRed and LeafGreen finally get Home support.

Once your game and Pokémon Home are linked, you can transfer your favorite little guys from FireRed and LeafGreen to Home and then to your other Pokémon games. Keep in mind that, just like when Pokémon Legends: Z-A got Home support, any Pocket Monster transferred from FireRed and LeafGreen to another game cannot go back to its original game.

So if you want to bring your FireRed Charizard on a little vacation to Lumiose City, know it won't be a temporary stay — that Charizard has a permanent home in Legends: Z-A now. Similarly, Pokémon from other games cannot be transferred to FireRed and LeafGreen.

Once you catch 'em all and connect Pokémon FireRed and/or Pokémon LeafGreen to Home, you'll be gifted a Celebi. Players who complete their game's Pokédex will then receive the Mythical Pokémon for free. You won't need to transfer your FR or LG Pokémon to Home to get the Celebi; the Pokémon registered in your Pokédex will then be registered in Home.

Game Freak and The Pokémon Company haven't specified the exact date Pokémon Home support will arrive as they've just given an October 2026 window. The update will also increase the number of Pokémon Premium Home subscribers can deposit from 6,000 to 9,000. Trainers will also be able to transfer Pokémon Go Pokémon that were caught with a Safari Ball to Home for the first time; the ball will switch to a Strange Ball.

Unfortunately, it's not all good news in the world of transferring Pokémon. The Nintendo 3DS app Pokémon Bank will be shut down on Feb. 25, 2027, at 10 p.m. EST. Trainers will then no longer be able to move Pokémon from Bank to Home past that date.

Log in before Sept. 6 to claim your reward
